findings.title: `tape_complete_through` field description contradicts the value it carries
findings.description: `TradesResponse.tape_complete_through` is documented as "Created time of the newest stored trade. Null means the trades phase has never run — not that the tape is empty today." The value actually served is `sync_state['trades'].watermark_ts` — the *end of the last fully walked window*, not the newest stored trade. The schema comment in `src/manta_trading/market/schema/migrations/kalshi.py` (kalshi_006) is explicit that this is "the tape is complete through this instant (end of the last fully walked window) - NOT the newest stored trade", and the slice design (D5) says the same. This matters because the field's whole job (D5) is to let a client distinguish "the window is past what the collector has reached" from "no activity in the window" — a description that says "newest stored trade" teaches a client the wrong inference rule for exactly the zero-count case the field exists to explain. The `CandlesResponse.complete_through` description gets this right ("Requested and stored through this instant — not 'the newest stored candle'"), so the two sibling fields disagree with each other as well. Fix the `tape_complete_through` description to match the watermark semantics.

findings.title: `TradeRecord.from_row` indexes row values positionally against an independently-ordered column list
findings.description: `TradeRecord.from_row` reads `values[0]`…`values[7]` positionally, while the SELECT projection is built from `TRADE_VALUE_COLUMNS` in `src/manta_trading/data/kalshi/serve_timeseries.py:44-47`, which is `tuple(column for column, _ in TRADE_COLUMNS if column != "market_ticker")`. The two orderings agree only by coincidence of the current `TRADE_COLUMNS` tuple; nothing enforces it. A column inserted or reordered in `TRADE_COLUMNS` (e.g. adding `taker_side` back, or moving `is_block_trade`) silently mis-maps every trade field on the wire — `created_time` would still be right only if it stays first, and `trade_id`/`count_fp`/prices would shift under it. The candle path does not have this problem: `CandleRecord.from_row` zips `row.values` against `CANDLE_COLUMNS` with `strict=True` and walks each column's declared attribute path, so a mapping change is caught by `zip(strict=True)` and by the parity test. The trade path should do the same — carry the column names with the row, or zip against a named tuple — rather than depending on positional agreement between two files.

findings.title: `tape_filtered` duplicates the exclusion-set comparison it claims not to
findings.description: `tape_filtered` renders `trades_filter_sql(excluded)` and then reads back `selection.params["trades_excluded_categories"]` to do a Python `in` test — so the membership test *is* effectively re-spelled in Python, even though the docstring says "The membership test is not re-spelled here." The current behaviour is correct (the integration test `TestTapeFiltered` verifies agreement with the rendered SQL across five configurations, including the `None` category and the empty-set case), and re-using the rendered parameter set does avoid a second source of truth for the *set*. But the function still depends on the SQL renderer's internal parameter name (`"trades_excluded_categories"`) and on `params` being empty exactly when the set is empty — a fragile coupling to an implementation detail of `selection.py`. A cleaner shape would expose the excluded set's membership as a small helper in `selection.py` next to `trades_filter_sql`, so both the SQL predicate and the Python predicate derive from one function. Not a defect; noting it because the docstring currently overstates the guarantee.

findings.title: Load-tier assertion 2 relies on a private psycopg pool attribute
findings.description: The "no row fetch ran" assertion reaches into `pool._pool` (`# noqa: SLF001`) to install the recording `ClientCursor` on live connections. This works today and the reasoning is sound (a `ClientCursor` renders client-side, so `mogrify` gives the statement the server sees, without a second round trip), but it depends on a psycopg_pool private attribute whose shape is not part of the public API and could change between psycopg_pool versions — the project pins `psycopg_pool>=3.2.0` with no upper bound. Worth an explicit comment naming the psycopg_pool version this was verified against, or a small compatibility shim, so a dependency bump surfaces here rather than as a silent loss of coverage. The test is skipped unless `MT_RUN_LOAD_TESTS=1`, so a break would not be noticed by ordinary CI.

findings.title: Window resolution is correctly extracted and shared, with the end-of-day convention preserved
findings.description: `windows.py` centralises the day-boundary convention that `bars.py` previously owned privately, and `bars.py` now imports `window_start_utc`/`window_end_utc` rather than restating them. The `end` bound remains inclusive at every granularity (`time.max`), the reversed-range message matches the bars route's wording and format, and a naive datetime is resolved to UTC deterministically rather than to the server's local zone. `resolve_window` raises before any database work, which the unit test `test_reversed_range_is_rejected_before_any_db_work` pins (`pool.checkouts == 0`). The `date | datetime` annotation with `# noqa: TC003` is required at runtime for FastAPI's query parsing and is documented inline.

findings.title: Count-first admission runs before any row fetch on both time-series routes
findings.description: The candlesticks and trades routes both seek the market, then count, then fetch — and the fetch is skipped when the count exceeds the ceiling. The over-ceiling `HTTPException` is raised *after* `run_in_executor` returns, so the pooled connection is already released when the 422 unwinds (pinned by `test_the_connection_is_released_before_the_refusal`, which asserts `pool.open_now == 0`). The readers build the count and fetch predicates from one `_window` helper, so they cannot drift, and neither carries a `LIMIT` — the documented trade-off being that a row inserted between count and fetch overshoots rather than under-shoots the ceiling. The ceiling itself comes from `get_max_bars` (the live setting), never a literal, and the 422 message quotes both the live count and the live ceiling.

findings.title: The tape floor is genuinely shared, not re-derived
findings.description: `_effective_floor` was promoted to the public `effective_tape_floor` in the same module and is now called from both `read_trade_status` (the CLI) and `serve_timeseries.tape_facts` (the API), so the two surfaces cannot report different floors — the exact risk the slice design named. The function's own query against the `historical` surface row is a single indexed read. The three branches (no historical row, older historical watermark, newer historical watermark) are each covered by a direct integration test in `TestEffectiveTapeFloor`, not only indirectly through the CLI.

findings.title: The load tier asserts the refusal property mechanically, not just by status code
findings.description: `test_over_ceiling_is_refused_without_fetching_rows` installs a recording cursor over the real pool and asserts that a `count(*)` against `kalshi.trades` ran *and* that no row-projecting `SELECT` against that table ran. A test asserting only the 422 status would pass even if the rows were read and discarded — this one does not, which is what D8 required. The fixture seeds `ceiling + 1,000` rows so both sides of the boundary are reachable from one fixture, and the window used by assertion 1 is derived from `API_MAX_BARS_PER_REQUEST` rather than written down, so raising the ceiling moves the window with it. The per-tier prod-URL guard in `test_167_data_status_nfr.py` still covers the new module (it globs every `*.py` in `test/load/`), and the new module never reads `MT_TIMESCALE_DB_URL` — `create_app(db_url=...)` is the seam.

structured_findings.summary: `tape_complete_through` field description contradicts the value it carries
`TradeRecord.from_row` indexes row values positionally against an independently-ordered column list
`tape_filtered` duplicates the exclusion-set comparison it claims not to
Load-tier assertion 2 relies on a private psycopg pool attribute
Window resolution is correctly extracted and shared, with the end-of-day convention preserved
Count-first admission runs before any row fetch on both time-series routes
The tape floor is genuinely shared, not re-derived
The load tier asserts the refusal property mechanically, not just by status code
